title: Andrea needs to understand GenAI
message: One student’s learning process, from assignment to assessment
body: Andrea is a second-year computer science student: he can program, but still confuses key concepts of generative models.
He must study a chapter and explain how a language model generates text.
We observe his use of tools and the evidence of understanding he keeps.
decision: You are following the learning method; you do not need to learn programming.

title: Andrea’s learning task
message: To understand the chapter and show what he has learned, Andrea must:

steps.title: Read
steps.text: Study the chapter. Identify the key ideas and what is still unclear.

steps.title: Represent
steps.text: Build a diagram with labelled links between the concepts.

steps.title: Check
steps.text: Compare the diagram and AI suggestions with the chapter. Correct errors.

steps.title: Explain
steps.text: Use his own words to explain a new example, without AI help.

decision: Evidence: a checked diagram, an independent explanation and a justified correction.

title: Self-directed learning: making choices
message: Andrea takes an active role: he identifies his learning needs, chooses a path and reviews his progress.

comparison.label: 1. Identify a goal
comparison.text: What do I need to learn, and what do I want to achieve?

comparison.label: 2. Choose a path
comparison.text: Which resources, people and strategies will help me learn?

comparison.label: 3. Review progress
comparison.text: What can I explain now, and what needs more work? Self-assessment helps here.

result: “I need to distinguish training from inference. I will use the chapter and a concept map, then check whether I can explain the difference.”
decision: Andrea takes responsibility for his choices, with support from teachers and peers.

title: Self-assessment: checking progress
message: Andrea judges his progress against clear criteria, then uses that judgement to improve his work.

comparison.label: 1. Check the criteria
comparison.text: What should I be able to explain or do?

comparison.label: 2. Look for evidence
comparison.text: What can I demonstrate? Where do I still struggle?

comparison.label: 3. Choose a next step
comparison.text: What will I revise, practise or check again?

result: “I can explain what a token is, but I still confuse training and inference. I will revise that link in my map and explain it again.”
decision: AI can offer feedback; the learner checks the evidence and decides what to improve.

title: A study process in six phases
message: Choose support for your next learning action. The corner ribbon shows the main phase, with a smaller secondary phase.

steps.title: PLAN
steps.text: Set your goal, identify your starting point and organise tasks and time.

steps.title: UNDERSTAND
steps.text: Clarify difficult ideas through explanations, examples and questions.

steps.title: CONNECT
steps.text: Explain ideas in your own words and organise relationships between concepts.

steps.title: RECALL
steps.text: Retrieve what you know without looking, then revisit it over time.

steps.title: APPLY
steps.text: Use what you have learned to solve problems and handle new situations.

steps.title: CHECK
steps.text: Compare your performance with criteria, identify gaps and decide what to study next.

decision: Checking guides your next step. SUPPORT marks setup, sources and sharing.

title: /quiz
message: Answer questions, review feedback and move through a quiz.

title: /flashcard
message: Practise recall with questions and answers on flip cards.
prompt: /flashcard Using only the attached chapter, create a compact three-card recall activity on tokens, context and probability versus truth. Use a self-contained inline worksheet widget in this ChatGPT response, independently usable from its shared link. Show one card at a time, Reveal/Hide answer, Previous/Next, I remember this/Needs practice, reviewed progress, summary, Review missed cards and Reset. Cite chapter sections and pages in each answer. Disable and visibly dim both rating buttons until the current answer is revealed, with “Reveal the answer before rating.” Count each card once; changing a rating replaces it; navigation preserves state. Missed-only review hides answers for fresh recall. When its last missed card becomes remembered, automatically show the updated summary; never show 0 of 0 or a fallback card. Reset everywhere clears ratings, reveals and review modes, returning to Question 1 with 0 of 3 reviewed. Use inline response controls rather than an account-saved deck, file or external app. Use English learner-facing text only.
decision: Scores reflect self-ratings. Cross-chat recall and daily scheduling were not tested.

message: Classify examples into categories and check the result.
prompt: /sortinggame Using only the attached chapter, build an interactive three-item sorting widget. Classify parameter updates, fixed-model calculations and adding prompt context as training or inference. Include checking and explanations. Answer in English.

Show exactly three selectable branches: Training, Inference and RAG. Selecting a branch must reveal its labelled relationships and a chapter-grounded explanation. Include three short check questions, one per branch, with answer choices, a Check answers button, explanatory feedback and a Retry control. Keep parameter updates separate from context changes. Use a compact native interactive widget, not an image. Answer in English.

Let the learner choose what changes in each scenario and use a Check answers button with explanatory feedback. Include a Reveal answers / Hide answers control for the answer key and one independent explanation check. Keep the controls in a compact interactive widget. Answer in English.

Include learner answer fields, a Check answers control where answers can be checked, Reveal answers / Hide answers, and completion progress. Keep one level visible at a time. Use a compact native interactive widget. Answer in English.

comparison.text: One arrow labelled “prompt → training → answer” mixes different processes.

comparison.label: Look for
comparison.text: Separate training; show a cycle for token-by-token inference.

decision: Explain each arrow, then check the inference cycle against the chapter.

title: draw.io: build the inference path
message: A student-built flow from the workshop book.
prompt: Using book §§1.2 and 1.7, build prompt + context → inference with fixed weights → next token. Explain what changes when a definition is added to the prompt.
decision: New context changes the input; ordinary inference keeps the learned parameters fixed.

title: Excalidraw: explain the RAG arrow
message: A freehand reconstruction of a relationship in §1.7.
prompt: Using book §1.7, sketch retrieved passages → prompt context. Label the arrow and add the limit: retrieval changes the context, not the model’s weights.
decision: Explain why an irrelevant retrieved passage can still produce an unreliable answer.

title: MindMeister: rebuild a branching map
message: Close the book, reconstruct one relationship, then reopen §§1.2 and 1.7 to check it.

comparison.label: MindMeister
comparison.text: Alternative for a branching mind map. Basic requires an account and allows three maps per person, including maps shared with you.

decision: Compare your reconstruction with the AI visual: identify one missing relationship and justify a correction.

title: The teacher designs the evidence
message: The goal, task and criterion must concern the same knowledge

comparison.label: Goal
comparison.text: Understand the roles of context, parameters and token selection.

comparison.label: Evidence
comparison.text: An explanation, commented diagram, justified prediction and correction.

comparison.label: Criteria
comparison.text: Concepts and relationships; process explanation; application and checking.

decision: Assess what the learner can justify, alongside the assisted product.

title: MagicSchool: draft and review a rubric
message: Generate three criteria and four levels; review the descriptors and export.
prompt: Create a four-level rubric for a second-year university student who studies the workshop chapter, builds a labelled diagram and independently explains language-model generation. Use exactly three criteria: concepts and relationships; process explanation; application and checking. Describe observable evidence at each level. Distinguish the assisted product from the independent explanation. Do not reward writing polish or code complexity alone. Source distinctions: training updates numerical parameters; ordinary inference uses fixed parameters; adding a prompt definition changes context; RAG supplies retrieved passages as context and does not itself update weights; next-token probability is not a guarantee of truth.

decision: Teacher check: distinguish context from parameters and assisted work from independent explanation.

title: MagicSchool: check questions and answers
message: Generate five questions, check the key and request missing explanations.
prompt: Create five questions on the supplied chapter summary for second-year university students. Test training versus inference, a definition added to a prompt, tokens versus words, RAG versus parameter updates, and next-token probability versus truth. Provide the answer key and a brief rationale. Avoid trick questions. Source summary: training changes parameters; ordinary inference uses fixed parameters; a new prompt changes context; a token may be a word, word part or punctuation; RAG supplies retrieved passages as context and does not guarantee correctness; token probability measures a possible continuation, not the factual truth of the whole answer. Answer in English. Keep questions concise and provide one short rationale per correct answer.
decision: Check each answer and its rationale against the chapter before assigning the questions.

title: Formative: build and preview an assessment
message: Build three questions, check the key and preview the learner’s view.
decision: Recorded in a Paid Teacher trial. The teacher checks the AI draft before learners see it.
prompt: Create three questions for a private workshop demonstration, in English. Use only these chapter facts: training updates model parameters; ordinary inference keeps parameters fixed; a new prompt changes context; RAG supplies retrieved passages as context. Q1 Multiple Choice: During ordinary inference, what changes when a new prompt is entered? Options: A The original training data; B The available context; C The learned parameters. Correct answer B, 1 point. Q2 Free Response: Andrea says that adding a definition to the prompt updates the model weights. Explain the error in two sentences. Expected: context changes, learned parameters remain fixed during ordinary inference. Q3 Drawing: Draw and label prompt plus context -> inference with fixed parameters -> next token. Add a brief note explaining what changes when a definition is added. Use only these three basic question types. This is an authored example; no real student records.

title: Activity: adapt an assessment
message: Five minutes on your subject and an access barrier

steps.title: Choose a goal · 1 minute
steps.text: Name a concept you teach or study.

steps.title: Design evidence · 2 minutes
steps.text: Write a task and observable criterion, allowing AI to produce the initial product.

steps.title: Remove a barrier · 2 minutes
steps.text: Offer an equivalent access or response option; share the reason for your choice.

decision: A reusable example with a coherent goal, evidence and support.

title: Reuse the learning path in another subject
message: Keep the sequence; change the content and evidence

steps.title: Start with a source and a goal
steps.text: For example: understand a historical interpretation from an assigned chapter.

steps.title: Make ideas visible
steps.text: Record an initial explanation, uncertainties and a manageable plan.

steps.title: Use tools, then check
steps.text: Compare a generated explanation with the source and revise relationships.

steps.title: Demonstrate and reflect
steps.text: Explain a new example independently; identify the next learning step.

decision: Choose a tool for a specific need and decide what evidence it should leave.

title: The evidence collected along the way
message: A product and an explanation answer different assessment needs

comparison.label: Learning process
comparison.text: Selected plan, checked passages, a generated Mind Map and self-check responses.

comparison.label: Assisted product
comparison.text: Diagram, checked study materials, practice responses and revision history.

comparison.label: Demonstrated knowledge
comparison.text: Independent explanation, prediction, error correction and reflection.

decision: Compare these records before deciding what the learner needs next.
